text: A full undergraduate quantum mechanics sequence runs two or three semesters, covering plenty of material you'll never touch as a quantum software engineer. This lesson draws the line explicitly: what's in this course, and what's deliberately left out.

This course will not grind through solving the Schrödinger equation for real atoms like hydrogen — a qubit's two-dimensional space is engineered by hardware teams, so you never re-derive it from a continuous potential. It skips perturbation theory, the toolkit for approximating messy real Hamiltonians, because quantum gates are exact operations you specify directly, not approximations. It skips Feynman's path-integral formulation, since the discrete circuit model never needs a sum over continuous trajectories. And it skips angular momentum coupling, which belongs to atomic and nuclear physics, not the finite-dimensional world of qubits.

What you do get, in full rigor: finite-dimensional complex vector spaces, the actual home of n qubits in a 2-to-the-n-dimensional space, with no differential equations required. Dirac notation, learned precisely rather than as vague shorthand. Superposition, measurement, and the Born rule. Entanglement, the resource multi-qubit algorithms depend on. And unitary evolution together with the no-cloning theorem, which has real, practical consequences for quantum cryptography and error correction.

Here's the one sentence that explains why this subset is exactly right: a quantum circuit is nothing but unitary operators applied to a finite-dimensional state, followed by a measurement — pure linear algebra, no continuous potentials, no perturbative approximations needed. Hardware teams engineer qubits specifically so software never has to leave that clean layer. And every topic this course does cover gets taught to the same rigor a physics major gets — exact statements, correct notation, no hand-waving. What's different is which topics make the cut, not how carefully the included ones are treated.
Next lesson is a check-yourself lab: a handful of applied scenarios that force you to actually use the foundations from this chapter, the way a colleague might ask you to explain them on the spot.
